title: Post-Diwali Reset Without Crash Diets: Experts Advise Habits Over Detox
excerpt: Doctors and dietitians quoted this week converge on the same prescription — regular meals, probiotic staples, post-meal walks and sleep — and against the detox products marketed every festival season.
body:
• Doctors and dietitians quoted this week give the same advice: skip crash diets and commercial detoxes, and return to regular, balanced meals, movement and sleep.
  • The British Dietetic Association calls detox diets "a marketing myth" — the liver, kidneys and gut already clear waste, a point repeated by wellness clinicians at GOQii.
  • A practical three-day reset from Dr Asjad Ahmed Khan: probiotic foods such as dahi, buttermilk and idli, 2.5-3 litres of water a day, a 20-30 minute walk after meals, and sleep by 10:30 p.m.
  • See a doctor rather than self-treating if acidity lasts more than five days, or with severe abdominal pain, blood in stool, vomiting, or no bowel movement for over three days. Readers with diabetes, kidney disease, IBS or other chronic conditions should check with their own doctor first.

The week after Diwali reliably produces two things: a fridge of leftover mithai and a flood of detox advice. The experts quoted in this week's coverage are unusually united against the second. Nutritionist Dr Sumaiya Petiwala told Mirror Now the focus should be consistency rather than drastic swings, warning that skipping meals leads to excessive hunger, energy crashes, acidity and later overeating. Dermatologist Dr Ritika Shanmugam, in the same report, attributed post-Diwali acne, dehydration and dull skin to firecracker smoke, pollution, inconsistent skincare, late nights and high-glycaemic food — and prescribed a gentle cleanser, moisturiser and broad-spectrum sunscreen over aggressive treatments, plus a gradual return to a consistent sleep-wake cycle of seven to nine hours a night.

What a gentle reset actually looks like

Dr Asjad Ahmed Khan, an Ayurveda and emergency-medicine practitioner quoted by HerZindagi, lays out a three-day version built on ordinary food rather than restriction: probiotic foods — dahi, buttermilk, idli and dosa — alongside prebiotic staples such as oats, banana, onion, garlic, legumes and vegetables; 2.5 to 3 litres of water a day; a 20-30 minute walk after meals; sleep by 10:30 p.m.; and a pause on fried, packaged and very spicy food. His red-flag list is the part worth keeping: acidity beyond five days, severe abdominal pain, blood in stool, vomiting, or no bowel movement for more than three days means a doctor, not a diet.

Why "detox" is the wrong frame

The physiological claim behind detox products does not hold up, as GOQii's clinical explainer notes: the liver, kidneys and gut already clear waste continuously, and the British Dietetic Association calls detox diets "a marketing myth." Rapid fasting losses are mainly water and glycogen, not fat. The scale, in any case, moves less than the guilt suggests — a US study published in the New England Journal of Medicine found average holiday weight gain of about 0.5 kg, though the study also found that gain is often not lost later, which is an argument for resuming normal habits promptly rather than for punishing ones.

"The liver, kidneys and gut already clear waste — detox diets are a marketing myth."

— British Dietetic Association position, via GOQii

The boring prescription

Put together, the expert advice is deliberately un-dramatic: eat regular, balanced meals instead of skipping them; reintroduce fibre through whole grains, millets, fruit and vegetables; hydrate with water and soups rather than commercial detox drinks; walk after meals; and fix the sleep schedule the festival broke. Readers managing diabetes, kidney disease, IBS, pregnancy or any chronic condition should treat all of the above as general information and check with their own doctor before changing diet or exercise — the one point on which every source, commercial or clinical, agrees.
